title: Peace with God (Romans 5:1–11)
hook: suffering, patience, character, hope; while we were still sinners, Christ died

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was faith, pistis, trust: an old man under the stars. Your line was counted as right.

Ask the steady one in your life how they got that way, the one people call at two in the morning. The answer is rarely: everything went well for me. More often it's: the year my dad was sick. The job I lost. The long winter after the divorce. Something hard happened, and something grew in the hard ground. Nobody chooses the hard part, but what grew is often what they'd keep. Paul knew this from the inside: shipwrecked, beaten, jailed, and still writing letters. In Romans chapter five he traces the pattern step by step, and he starts somewhere surprising: with peace.
screen: `HOW DID THEY GET THAT WAY?` → `SOMETHING HARD HAPPENED.` → `PAUL STARTS WITH PEACE.`

segments.voice: Chapter five opens, in the King James Bible: "Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ." The Greek word for peace is eirene, and behind it stands the Hebrew shalom: not just no fighting, but wholeness, everything in its right place. After four chapters about guilt and grace, the war is over. Then Paul does something odd. He says we glory, even boast, in tribulations. Not because suffering is good, but because of what can grow in it: "tribulation worketh patience; And patience, experience; and experience, hope: And hope maketh not ashamed." Four links. Hard times grow endurance. Endurance grows what the King James calls experience; the Greek means tested character, like metal that's been through the fire and proved true. That tested character grows hope, and hope, Paul says, doesn't let you down. Maketh not ashamed echoes Paul's opening a few days ago: not ashamed. Why doesn't it disappoint? Because the love of God has been poured into our hearts. Then the line that holds the chapter up: "But God commendeth his love toward us, in that, while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us." Not after we got better. While. Paul notes that hardly anyone would die even for a righteous person. This love didn't wait for anyone to deserve it. Some readers say the chain is easier to see looking back than from the middle of it.
screen: `EIRENE: SHALOM, WHOLENESS.` · `GLORY IN TRIBULATIONS.` · `PATIENCE, TESTED CHARACTER, HOPE.` · `WHILE WE WERE YET SINNERS.` · then, large: `HOPE MAKETH NOT ASHAMED.`

segments.voice: Go back through your life slowly and find one hard season that, looking back, grew something in you: patience, compassion, honesty, a friend you'd never have met. Don't pretend it was good, it may still hurt; just name the hardship and what grew, and if one you're in right now comes instead, let it be there without forcing a lesson on it yet. If you pray, give thanks for what grew, and ask for hope in what hasn't yet.
Eirene. Paul's Greek word for peace, carrying the Hebrew shalom: wholeness, the war over, everything in its right place.
Your line: hope does not disappoint. The war is over, even in hard ground. Day three hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Christians often turn to Romans 5:1–5 in illness or loss; chaplains and friends read it with people in a hard season, and look back together on what that season grew.

chat.says: How can Paul say he's glad about hard times? Isn't that strange?
options: Not because suffering is good, but for what can grow in it: endurance, character, hope.
Because suffering is good in itself, so we ought to go looking for more of it.
Because he had found a way never to feel any pain or sadness again.
chat.meaning: Paul says tribulation grows patience, tested character and hope, and hope doesn't disappoint, because God's love is poured into our hearts.

notes: Romans 5:1 textual variant: echōmen ('let us have peace') vs. echomen ('we have peace'); many early manuscripts read the subjunctive, while most modern editions print the indicative. Trapdoor mentions this; confirm phrasing.

Link between 'hope maketh not ashamed' (5:5) and 'not ashamed' (1:16): both use a form of the verb for shame (kataischunō / epaischunomai); the script calls it 'the same phrase', which is loose. Confirm or soften to 'the same idea'.
Dokimē glossed as tested character, like proven metal; standard lexical sense. Confirm.
Care taken not to present suffering as good or as sent to teach; confirm the tone is pastorally sound.
